newsitem.title: USA: Fed candidate Ferguson to bring banking expertise.
newsitem.headline: Fed candidate Ferguson to bring banking expertise.

text.p: Roger W. Ferguson, Jr., a White House candidate for one of two vacant governor seats at the Federal Reserve Board, is a realist who will bring much-needed expertise in banking.
Ferguson, 45, an African-American born in Washington, D.C., has been a partner at the New York-based international consultancy firm McKinsey and Co Inc. since 1991.
Ferguson began working for McKinsey as a consultant in 1984, specializing in management strategies in areas including the increasingly deregulated U.S. banking sector.
"The Fed has been looking for someone with an expertise in banking for a long time, in fact since (Fed Governor John) LaWare left," a source close to the Fed said.
"It's particularly important for the Fed to have a banker at this juncture due to new regulations and technology-driven changes in the industry," the source added.
The Fed, one of the U.S. bank regulators, has found it difficult in the past to attract bankers due to potential conflicts of interests.
LaWare, the last bank expert at the Board, left in 1995 and was replaced by economist Laurence Meyer.

"The Fed will find in Roger Ferguson somebody who is very knowledgeable about banking and also very good at problem solving. The Fed is dealing with rather complex problems," a McKinsey executive told Reuters, referring to the role of the Fed in the U.S. payments system.

Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan last year appointed a special commission, headed by Fed Vice Chair Alice Rivlin, to look into the role the Fed should play in providing financial services to a banking industry that is rapidly evolving due to new regulations and advanced technology.
"Ferguson was trained as a consultant to deal with those kind of problems," the McKinsey executive added. "And he is a wonderful academic."

Ferguson earned a PhD in economics from Harvard University and wrote his dissertation on joint ventures in the manufacturing sector. He also holds a law degree from Harvard, and practiced as an attorney with the firm of Davis Polk & Wardwell, specializing in corporate mergers and public offerings.
McKinsey, a firm with 600 partners and 3,400 consultants in 39 countries, said Ferguson, as director of research and information, also played a role in the company's strategy.
If appointed, Ferguson, the son of an Army map-maker and a school teacher, will become only the third African-American in the central bank's 84-year history to sit on the seven-member Fed Board.
The Fed routinely has come under criticism by civil rights advocates for insufficient minority representation, a record that President Bill Clinton has vowed to improve.
Clinton last year named Rivlin as the first woman vice chair of the Fed, bringing to an unprecedented three the number of women sitting simultaneously at the Board.
The two other African-Americans to have served as Fed governors were also appointed by Democratic presidents.
"Emmett Rice was an appointee of (President Jimmy) Carter and Andrew Brimmer was appointed by (President Lyndon) Johnson," a former Fed official told Reuters.
Rice was Fed governor from 1979 to 1986 and Brimmer from 1966 to 1974.
"Somehow, it has always seemed difficult for the Fed to find minorities to fill these positions. But Ferguson is a great choice (given) his all-around expertise," the former Fed official said.
Congressman Henry Gonzalez (D-Texas), has regularly criticized the Fed for offering too few opportunities to minorities.
A spokeswoman at Gonzalez's office said the congressman, who is the ranking Democrat on the House Banking Committee, was not available for comment but would certainly welcome Clinton's choice.

Two other Fed governors, Janet Yellen and Lawrence Lindsey, left earlier this year. Besides Ferguson, the White House also is expected to nominate University of Michigan Professor of Economics Edward Gramlich to the Fed Board.
